French abstract:
Malgré l’augmentation du nombre de médecins, des investissements importants et de multiples changements structurels, les réformes des soins primaires au Québec au cours des deux dernières décennies ont entraîné des améliorations limitées de l’accès. Près d’un quart des Québécois n’ont toujours pas de médecin de famille, et les urgences demeurent fortement sollicitées par des cas qui pourraient être pris en charge en soins primaires.

Des politiques coercitives telles que les régimes régionaux de dotation médicale, le travail hospitalier obligatoire et des lois récentes comme les projets de loi 83 et 2 ont rendu la médecine familiale moins attrayante, éloignant les nouveaux diplômés et réduisant le temps clinique que les médecins de famille consacrent aux soins primaires complets.

Les équipes de soins de santé, introduites par l’entremise des groupes de médecine de famille, n’ont pas atteint tout leur potentiel en raison d’incitatifs mal harmonisés, d’un partage limité des tâches et d’un modèle de rémunération à l’acte. Par conséquent, la capacité des médecins est sous-utilisée, et les professionnels non médecins restent insuffisamment intégrés.

L’amélioration durable nécessite une réforme structurelle coordonnée : passer à des modèles de paiement par capitation ajustés en fonction du risque, imposer l’inscription des patients avec une responsabilité claire, intégrer pleinement le personnel infirmier praticien et les pharmaciens dans les équipes de soins, et établir des systèmes solides de mesure du rendement avec des rapports publics transparents.

English abstract: 
Despite increased physician supply, substantial investment, and multiple structural changes, Quebec’s primary care reforms over the past two decades have yielded limited improvements in access. Over one-quarter of Quebecers still lack a regular provider, and emergency rooms remain heavily burdened by primary-care-treatable cases. 

Coercive policies such as regional medical staffing plans, mandatory hospital work, and recent legislation like Bills 83 and 2 have made family medicine less attractive, driving new graduates away and reducing the clinical time family doctors spend on comprehensive primary care. 

Team-based care, introduced through family medicine groups, has not reached its potential due to misaligned incentives, limited task-sharing, and a fee-for-service payment model. As a result, physician capacity is underused and non-physician professionals remain insufficiently integrated. 

Sustainable improvement requires coordinated, structural reform. This includes transitioning to risk-adjusted capitation payment models, fully integrating nurse practitioners and pharmacists into care teams, mandating patient enrollment with clear accountability, and establishing robust performance measurement systems with transparent public reporting.

title: Assessing the Influence of the Urban Ecosystem Services on Urban Quality of Life: A Comprehensive Study of Khulna City, Bangladesh
affiliations: Lund University, Khulna University and Khulna University

detail.title: Assessing the Influence of the Urban Ecosystem Services on Urban Quality of Life: A Comprehensive Study of Khulna City, Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization in developing countries, particularly in cities like Khulna, Bangladesh, is exerting significant pressure on urban ecosystems and hindering improvements in urban quality of life (UQoL). Despite the city’s valuable natural resources, residents face low livelihood and well-being indicators, highlighting the need to better understand the link between ecosystem services (ES) and UQoL. This study classified Khulna into six urban ecosystem categories and used a combination of household surveys and focus group discussions (FGDs) to collect primary data. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) prioritized indicators of ES supply and UQoL demand, while Kendall’s coefficient of concordance measured agreement, and gap analysis quantified discrepancies between available and expected UQoL. The study found that unplanned residential areas (URA) possess stronger provisioning and regulating services compared with other residential zones, while cultural services, particularly social relationships comprising 45–73% of criteria weight (Cw) across all areas. Physical, social, and psychological health (PH, SH, and PsH) services were oversupplied by the ecosystems in most areas, yet economic health requirements remain deficient in slum residential areas (SRA) and a latent undervaluation of existing services has emerged in the most non-residential areas. In the study UQoL rankings revealed low agreement (Kendall’s W = 0.011, χ² = 0.2), signifying that residents are more attuned to deficiencies than to the benefits they receive. This study exposes the resolve between ES supply and perceived UQoL demand exhibiting the lack of awareness with context-specific planning undermines the potential of urban ecosystems to improve residents’ well-being. It recommends targeted green–blue infrastructure, and community awareness programs to bridge this diversion and enhance livelihood quality in Khulna City and comparable rapidly urbanizing cities.

detail.title: New Wine in Old Wineskins Unintended Financial Dominance and Central Banking Myopia
detail.abstract: This paper provides a positive analysis of the links between macroeconomic fundamentals, unintended financial dominance, and central banking myopia. When current levels of public and private leverage depend on past monetary and supervisory policies, the risk of financial dominance is itself shaped by past policy choices, with expectations acting as the intertemporal transmission mechanism. Expectations incorporate the perceived likelihood of future financial dominance through two channels: a de jure capture bias and a de facto accommodation bias. In this setting, central banking myopia becomes an endogenous outcome of the regime, and financial dominance is unintended. The theoretical framework is used to interpret post-Global Financial Crisis reforms in central bank design as manifestations of stronger capture bias, and the widespread use of unconventional monetary policies as evidence of stronger accommodation bias.

detail.title: Protecting Electoral Integrity and Democracy: Addressing the Threat of Malign Foreign Influence and Interference in the Philippines' 2025 Midterm Elections
detail.abstract: As geopolitical tensions in the Indo-Pacific intensify, the Philippines faces mounting challenges both from external coercion at sea and from malign foreign influence and interference targeting its democratic institutions. These operations manifest through multiple entry points, including the co-optation of local officials, organized crime, espionage, and election interference. This study examines the interplay between national and subnational governance in addressing these threats, using the 2025 Philippine midterm elections as case analysis. It highlights the constitutional tension between the President’s centralized authority over foreign policy and national security, and the constitutional autonomy of local governments. This tension creates opportunities for malign foreign actors to exploit subnational spaces through sister-city partnerships, economic incentives, and digital influence campaigns. Drawing on open-source data, key informant interviews, and spatial mapping, the study identifies geographic patterns of vulnerability. It analyzes the structural weaknesses that are susceptible to foreign interference in national and local institutions. The findings reveal that while national frameworks exist, uneven implementation at the subnational level heightens susceptibility to external manipulation. The study proposes two policy directions: enhancing subnational resilience through stronger oversight and stakeholder collaboration, and reinforcing electoral safeguards through legislative reform and the designation of a Counter Foreign Interference Coordinator under the office of the National Security Adviser. Addressing malign foreign influence and interference demands synchronized action across governance levels and a whole-of-society approach to safeguarding Philippine democracy.

detail.title: A Comparative Technical and Economic Analysis of Railway Track Superstructures: Ballasted, Ballastless, and Frame Sleeper Systems
detail.abstract: The selection of an appropriate railway track superstructure is a critical decision in modern infrastructure planning, with profound implications for operational performance, long-term economic viability, and network availability. This report presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the three principal track superstructure designs: traditional ballasted track, advanced ballastless (slab) track, and the emerging hybrid frame sleeper system. The study's methodology is a qualitative review of existing academic literature and technical reports, synthesizing data on design principles, construction, maintenance requirements, geometric stability, service life, and economic models. Key findings reveal a fundamental trade-off: ballasted track offers a lower initial capital expenditure but incurs high life cycle costs due to a perpetual cycle of maintenance required to correct geometric instability. Conversely, ballastless track demands a significantly higher upfront investment but delivers superior geometric stability, a substantially longer service life, and minimal maintenance, making it the economically and technically superior solution for high-speed and high-density corridors. The report concludes that there is no single universal solution; the optimal choice is contingent upon a strategic assessment of specific operational demands, geological conditions, and longterm financial objectives.

detail.title: Legal Alignment for Safe and Ethical AI
detail.abstract: Alignment of artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses the normative problem of specifying how AI systems should act and the technical problem of ensuring AI systems comply with those specifications. To date, AI alignment has generally overlooked an important source of knowledge and practice for grappling with these problems: law. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by exploring how legal rules, principles, and methods can be leveraged to address problems of alignment and inform the design of AI systems that operate safely and ethically. This emerging field — legal alignment — focuses on three research directions: (1) designing AI systems to comply with the content of legal rules developed through legitimate institutions and processes, (2) adapting methods from legal interpretation to guide how AI systems reason and make decisions, and (3) harnessing legal concepts as a structural blueprint for confronting challenges of reliability, trust, and cooperation in AI systems. These research directions present new conceptual, empirical, and institutional questions, which include examining the specific set of laws that particular AI systems should follow, creating evaluations to assess their legal compliance in real-world settings, and developing governance frameworks to support the implementation of legal alignment in practice. Tackling these questions requires expertise across law, computer science, and other disciplines, offering these communities the opportunity to collaborate in designing AI for the better.

title: Why Supply Chains Need AI, More than Ever?

detail.title: Why Supply Chains Need AI, More than Ever?
detail.abstract: Supply chains have never been simple. From sourcing raw materials to delivering finished goods to consumers, the processes involve many stages, actors, and dependencies often across countries, time zones, and regulatory environments. In a world with volatile demand, unpredictable disruptions (e.g. natural disasters, pandemics, geopolitical events), and increasing customer expectations (faster delivery, better traceability), traditional supply chain approaches are struggling to keep up. This is where AI enters not as a futuristic luxury but as a strategic necessity. By processing large, complex data sets, learning from patterns, and making predictions or decisions more quickly than humans, AI promises to transform supply chain management from reactive and manual to proactive, dynamic, and resilient. In doing so, AI changes not only how supply chains operate operationally, but also how managers think about uncertainty, risk, and opportunity. In this essay, I examine the multifaceted impacts of AI on supply chains: what it's good at, where it struggles, real world applications, and the human/organizational challenges that accompany it.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how sovereign default risk, measured by the Emerging Market Bond (EMBI) Index, affects the composition of central bank reserves, with a particular focus on gold holdings. Using a panel of 52 countries from 1997 to 2020, the study employs dynamic panel GMM, local projections, and instrumental-variable Tobit estimators to examine the response of the gold share of central bank reserves to changes in sovereign default risk. Leveraging a newly constructed dataset on country-level reserve currency composition, the analysis disentangles portfolio reallocation toward gold from valuation-driven changes in gold shares. The results show that a surge in sovereign default risk is associated with a significant reallocation of reserves toward gold, consistent with a precautionary reserve management rationale. Local projection estimates indicate that the increase in gold share following a default risk shock persists for up to two years. The effect is stronger in countries with fixed exchange rate regimes and in those with lower central bank independence. Additionally, the analysis documents that higher U.S. dollar and special drawing right (SDR) debt composition is associated with an increase in the gold share of central bank reserves, highlighting the role of currency mismatches in shaping reserve allocation decisions.

title: Impact of AI on Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh

detail.title: Impact of AI on Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping global supply chains by improving forecasting accuracy, operational efficiency, quality consistency, and decision-making speed. For Bangladesh—whose economy is heavily dependent on the Ready-Made Garments (RMG) sector—the integration of AI represents a critical opportunity to strengthen competitiveness and meet rising expectations from global buyers. This paper investigates the current state of AI adoption in Bangladeshi supply chains, highlights key applications such as demand forecasting, computer-vision-based quality inspection, predictive maintenance, logistics optimization, sustainability analytics, and supplier evaluation, and assesses the associated economic and social impacts. Drawing from industry reports and recent trends, the study finds that although large RMG firms are increasingly investing in automation and analytics, overall adoption remains at an early stage due to skill shortages, weak digital infrastructure, fragmented supplier networks, and high capital requirements. The paper further outlines the risks of workforce displacement and data governance challenges. Finally, it proposes a policy and business roadmap focusing on skills development, SME financing, interoperable data standards, ethical AI governance, and inclusive automation strategies. The findings contribute to the growing literature on AI-enabled supply chains in developing economies and offer evidence-based recommendations for accelerating Bangladesh’s transition toward resilient, technology-driven manufacturing.

detail.abstract: The growing complexity of global supply networks has made supplier evaluation a strategic priority for firms seeking to manage risk, improve quality, and secure reliable sourcing. While several quantitative and qualitative models exist, many organizations still struggle to integrate subjective managerial judgments with objective performance data in a consistent and transparent manner. This study proposes a hybrid evaluation framework that combines the strengths of Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), and unsupervised learning techniques. The study highlights the potential of data-driven hybrid models to enhance supplier management practices in modern supply chains.

detail.abstract: As cybersecurity threats grow in complexity and frequency, protecting aircraft supply chains has become a pressing priority. In this work, we propose an integrated model-based systems engineering and optimization approach that captures all necessary information, including structure, behavior, requirements, and relevant parameters related to the acquisition process and supply chain. The approach also enables optimal supplier selection to reduce costs, maximize profits, and fulfill customer requirements under both deterministic and two-stage stochastic settings. Furthermore, it accounts for cybersecurity risks, such as data breaches, data corruption, IoT device compromise, and network intrusions, by modeling various attack scenarios and their consequences, allowing the manufacturer to make informed decisions under diverse conditions. Numerical tests demonstrate the model’s effectiveness, with the rate of requirement fulfillment under the attack scenarios showing a 50\% improvement over a deterministic approach. To be optimally equipped even for low-probability high-cost attack scenarios, we incorporate the risk measure Conditional Value-at-Risk. The resulting supplier selection process led to savings in the average expected cost across all attack scenarios, and a reduction in the maximum possible loss when these attacks are realized. The robustness of the proposed approach is demonstrated by its consistent performance across a range of scenarios and risk preferences, establishing it as a reliable tool for strengthening cybersecurity in aircraft supply chains.

detail.abstract: In low-defect manufacturing, automated release policies often fall into the “False Yield” trap, where high throughput masks unacceptable defect escape rates due to extreme class imbalance and board-level sparsity. To resolve these epistemic pathologies, this work proposes a Unified Frozen Knowledge-Based Conformal Policy, an auditable framework enforcing strict EvalDeploy consistency to bridge the gap between theoretical domain knowledge and industrial safety standards. The pipeline integrates three novel mechanisms: (a) UCB-Fair Gating, which fuses Bayesian Jeffreys priors with fairness regularization to act as a mathematical “safety valve” against distribution shift; (b) DAHCP-GCR, which leverages Manifold-Aware Knowledge Smoothing to resolve coverage collapse on cold-start boards without requiring large local calibration sets; and (c) HDEF, a defect routing mechanism featuring an Explicit Knowledge Guardrail (Singleton Safety Trap) to optimize the Intelligent Decision Support loop. Extensive experiments on a large-scale proprietary SMT dataset demonstrate that this unified policy effectively resolves the safety-efficiency-fairness trilemma. Under a unified global risk budget, it suppresses the Defect Escape Rate to ~3,021 ppm (strictly within the 5,000 ppm industrial limit) while maintaining a competitive Automated Yield of 88.2%. Crucially, it stabilizes the Worst-Board Coverage at 0.85 (vs. 0.84 for Global CP), ensuring equitable quality assurance across diverse product mixes. detail.abstract: This study implements, in a global setting, the financial statement benchmarking methodology proposed in Hoitash, Hoitash, Kurt, and Verdi (2023. The Accounting Review 98, 253) to construct a measure of international financial statement benchmarking (IFSB). IFSB is a scalable metric that quantifies the proportion of overlapping financial statement items reported by a firm and its global industry peers, providing a systematic method for assessing the availability of comparable benchmarking data worldwide. The central premise is that IFSB captures the ease with which market participants can perform line-by-line peer comparisons across borders. Validation tests show that analysts are more likely to co-cover international firms with higher IFSB, and boards are more likely to select international compensation peers with higher IFSB. At the firm level, analyses reveal that higher IFSB is associated with narrower bid-ask spreads, lower idiosyncratic risk, lower dispersion in analysts’ stock price forecasts, and greater value relevance of earnings, consistent with lower information acquisition and processing costs in international markets. By extending the existing benchmarking methodology to a global context and documenting additional capital market implications, this study offers new insights into peer benchmarking and the informativeness of international financial statement data.

detail.abstract: Governance is an essential component of effective national cancer control plan (NCCP) development and implementation and this study aims to describe how and the extent to which governance is defined and outlined in NCCPs. Findings show dynamic ancillary pricing delivers +17-58% conversion and +10-43% revenue per offer; conversational AI reduces waiting time up to 80% for routine intents but requires hybrid escalation to sustain NPS; recommenders raise CTR (~+15%) yet need stronger causal links to repeat booking and CLV; revenue-management accuracy improves +14-22%, supporting yield stability. Evidence remains limited on causal bridges to RASK/CASK and CO₂/ASK. Theoretically, we formalize a five-layer KPI architecture and position digital maturity as a measurable moderator. Practically, we recommend a Foundations → Pilot → Scale → Optimize roadmap with per-pax/per-ASK denominators, instrumentation (A/B, DiD, uplift), and responsible-AI gates (consent, bias, robustness, model cards). The framework enables airline leaders to convert AI initiatives into decision-grade, auditable value.

Many law school faculty are concerned that students may misuse artificial intelligence (AI) tools to undermine their learning and violate academic integrity policies.  Although some students will inevitably cheat, faculty can reduce the risk – and improve student learning – by rethinking assignment design and classroom communication.

detail.abstract:
The United States is accelerating toward a corruption crisis of its own making. In its race to rapidly acquire artificial intelligence (AI), current policy risks undermining longstanding procurement integrity safeguards. This article examines how AI increases traditional corruption risks and introduces new vulnerabilities that current oversight mechanisms are ill-equipped to address.  

Recent federal AI policies have accelerated adoption while simultaneously narrowing regulatory oversight, effectively leaving “regulation by contract” as the primary—and profoundly inadequate—mechanism for embedding safeguards. The consequence of these policies is that the government is “buying blind,” acquiring AI technologies without adequate transparency, audit rights, or testing requirements. These acquisition-phase deficiencies will translate directly into operational risks as AI deployment expands. How the government acquires AI today determines the procurement integrity vulnerabilities it will inherit tomorrow.

This article offers practical recommendations to address these emerging threats, prioritizing those most feasible to implement. It also challenges the assumption driving current federal AI policy: that governance impedes innovation. As the article demonstrates, governance is crucial for sustainable innovation. It helps maintain fair, transparent markets and fosters the institutional trust necessary for long-term AI integration.  

The window for establishing effective governance is closing. As procurement dependencies solidify and integrity risks become entrenched, reversing course will become exponentially harder.

title: Equity Blind Spots: How Health Programmes Fail Marginalized Populations Despite Good Policy Intentions

detail.abstract:
Introduction: Marginalized populations continue to experience persistent barriers to care, even in health systems where equity and universal access are explicit policy goals. Health policies across diverse health systems increasingly articulate strong commitments to equity, inclusion, and universal access, yet these intentions frequently fail to translate into equitable outcomes in practice. This paradox raises a critical policy question: why do well-designed health policies fail to produce equitable results? This paper examines equity failure not as a problem of policy intent, but as a systemic issue embedded within the policy–practice continuum of health programmes.

Methods: This paper adopts a conceptual analytical approach, drawing on established health equity and health systems scholarship to examine recurring patterns through which equity objectives are weakened during programme delivery. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the analysis synthesises theoretical and empirical insights from public health literature to identify mechanisms that systematically disadvantage marginalized populations.

Results: The analysis identifies four interrelated equity blind spots that recur across health programmes: (1) implicit assumptions of system capacity that obscure real-world constraints; (2) reliance on informal decision-making at service delivery points, which amplifies exclusion; (3) organisational and behavioural dynamics that deprioritize equity in favour of procedural compliance; and (4) ostensibly neutral administrative and technological systems that reproduce existing social and geographic inequalities. Together, these blind spots render inequity routine, normalized, and difficult to detect within standard performance assessments.

Discussion and Conclusion: The findings suggest that equity failures in health programmes are not anomalous but structurally produced. When equity is treated as an assumed outcome rather than an explicit analytical concern, programmes risk reinforcing the very disparities they aim to address. Addressing equity blind spots requires reframing equity as a core analytical dimension of policy effectiveness, with implications for how health programmes are designed, monitored, and assessed. Without such reframing, good policy intentions alone are unlikely to yield equitable health outcomes.

detail.abstract: Does proactive personality always enhance job success? The authors of this study draw on socioanalytic theory of personality and organizational political perspectives to study employees' political skill in moderating the effects of proactive personality on supervisory ratings of employee task performance, helping behaviors, and learning behaviors. Multisource data from 225 subordinates and their 75 immediate supervisors reveal that proactive personality is associated negatively with supervisory evaluations when political skill is low, and the negative relationship disappears when political skill is high. Implications and future research directions are discussed.

detail.title: Goal Choices and Planning: Distinct Expectancy and Value Effects in Two Goal Processes
detail.abstract: Expectancy and value have emerged as two major determinants of motivation. However, the exact nature of their functioning is less clear given that previous research failed to test adequately different goal processes. Based on the recent nonmonotonic, discontinuous model of expectancy elaborated by Vancouver, More, and Yoder (2008), two studies were conducted and found that expectancy and value functions in different forms during the goal choice versus goal planning processes. Specifically, the two constructs positively and jointly predicted one's goal choice, whereas they played independent and opposite roles in affecting the allocation of effort during the goal-planning process. These findings address gaps in theories of motivation, allow for more precise specifications of the roles for expectancy and value within such models, and further efforts toward integrating theories of motivation within a goal-centered, self-regulation framework.

detail.abstract: The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) plays a crucial role in inter-domain routing across the global internet. However, its static and manual policy configurations often lead to suboptimal route selection, resulting in inefficiencies in terms of bandwidth utilization, network resilience, and latency. Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers an innovative solution for optimizing BGP policy decisions, enabling adaptive, real-time route adjustments based on dynamic network conditions. This paper explores the application of Reinforcement Learning-based BGP policy optimization for Autonomous Systems (ASs) in the context of global internet routing. The study investigates how RL can be employed to automate and improve routing decisions by enabling BGP to self-learn optimal policies based on performance metrics such as throughput, latency, and fault tolerance. We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of RL in improving network resilience and route efficiency in autonomous systems while discussing the challenges and future directions for deploying RL-based BGP optimizations in large-scale networks

detail.abstract: Innovation rarely emerges within a single, stable "phase" of an organization or industry. Instead, breakthrough and structural innovations arise at the interfaces where fundamentally different logics, paradigms, and cultural systems collide. This paper introduces Ye-Jie-a generative boundary space formed through multi-phase aggregation, tension, and controlled elevation of energy and constraints. It argues that Ye-Jie is not a metaphorical abstraction, but a complex adaptive system created through designed organizational conditions. The paper theorizes the mechanisms by which Ye-Jie emerges and explains why this space becomes the origin of new structures, new paradigms, and new growth curves.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how knowledge is verified, debated, and circulated. As AI systems increasingly perform two traditionally human-centered peer review functions—logical coherence checking and computational verification—the epistemic legitimacy of conventional peer review requires re-examination. This paper offers a conditional account of peer review’s future: if AI remains stable, reliable, and publicly accessible, the role of peer review is likely to contract toward domains where epistemic judgment intersects with non-negotiable public risk (e.g., medicine, public health, nuclear engineering, and high-stakes AI governance). Outside these risk-intensive fields, knowledge verification will be increasingly supported by AI-enabled structural review, open dissemination platforms (e.g., SSRN, arXiv, Zenodo), and iterative transparency—shifting scholarly practice from an approval-based model to an iteration-based one. The paper further argues that framework-based theories grounded in axioms, operators, and formal or geometric structures are especially compatible with this environment because their internal logic is machine-verifiable and their extension mechanisms are transparent. All claims are explicitly conditional on AI stability; if this condition fails, the analysis requires full re-evaluation.

The team blends supervised learning architectures with SHAP and other explainable-AI techniques, and pairs those models with workflow automation tools that help generate evidence, triage cases, and route decisions where they need to go (Amebleh & Okoh, 2023). The upshot? The combined framework shows strong predictive chops, speeds up dispute turnaround times, and brings more operational clarity by exposing which factors drive the model's choices so you actually know why something was flagged or not (Alonge et al., 2021). Put simply: making these systems interpretable isn't just a nice-to-have. It appears to meaningfully boost trust, accountability, and overall effectiveness across financial dispute ecosystems (Rehan, 2021).

Zero-Touch Self-Healing BGP architectures present a novel approach that enables autonomous, dynamic network adjustments without manual intervention. detail.abstract: The article analyses the normatively and organisationally described models of training specialists in clinical psychology in the United Kingdom, the United States, and selected EU countries, and compares them with the current approaches used in Ukraine. The theoretical framework is based on a comparison of three regulatory frameworks for training quality: (1) requirements for basic psychological education and programme accreditation, (2) the core competencies of professional training and requirements for training content, (3) minimum standards for supervised clinical practice and mechanisms for admission to professional activity (registration/licensing/protected titles). It has been shown that in systems with the highest regulatory transparency, clinical psychology is typically grounded in long-term postgraduate training and structured supervision. In contrast, in Ukraine, entry paths are possible through a limited scope of specialisation in the absence of strictly defined boundaries of practice. In these systems, specialisation in clinical psychology is not usually achieved through short-term retraining or "additional specialisation", but rather through standardised requirements for training content, competencies, and practical experience. On this basis, the thesis of the risk of "role equivalence" is justified: some of the actual functions of a Ukrainian "clinical psychologist" may be similar to the profile of a Psychological Wellbeing Practitioner (PWP) in the British stepped-care model (low-intensity interventions for mild to moderate conditions), but without fully replicating the quality control infrastructure (standardised supervision, case routing, outcome monitoring). An approach to implementing international experience in Ukraine through a dual-track training architecture is proposed: a separate PWP-level role standard for low-intensity interventions and an expanded minimum framework for clinical psychologists (disciplines/ECTS/hours, mandatory supervised practice, and a competence verification mechanism).

This study examines the financial structure of the current artificial intelligence
investment cycle and evaluates whether the sector exhibits bubble-like vulnerabilities.
Using firm-level financial data, AI-exposure metrics, and scenario-based stress

detail.abstract: This work digs into how reinforcement-learning (RL) based optimization can actually improve decision-making in messy, fast-changing networked systems the kind where traditional heuristics tend to choke on scale and uncertainty (Papadis & Tassiulas). The core idea is simple-ish: instead of leaning on hand-crafted analytical models, the framework uses model-free RL to learn adaptive control policies straight from interacting with the system (Kadry). You let the agent try things, see what happens, and it figures out what works over time. In experiments, the RL agent didn't just match baseline methods, it consistently beat them on throughput, latency and how efficiently resources were allocated. That held up even when conditions drifted and the environment wasn't stationary, which is actually pretty encouraging (Chen et al.). Another key takeaway: feeding back environmental signals into the loop lets performance keep improving as the system changes, so this really fits data-driven, real-world settings where behavior evolves over time (Narayan et al.). All told, the study has solid, practical implications for managing large-scale infrastructure. It points toward deploying smarter, self-tuning systems across communications networks, cloud services and cyber-physical setups you know, places where automation that adapts on the fly is actually useful (Papadis & Tassiulas; Kadry; Chen et al.; Narayan et al.).

title: Blockchain-Based Regulatory Compliance Layer for U.S. Payments Using Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)

detail.title: Blockchain-Based Regulatory Compliance Layer for U.S. Payments Using Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)
detail.abstract: I took a close look at what a blockchain-based compliance layer might actually do for U.S. payment systems using zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) as the key ingredient. The study lays out a conceptual model, grounded in current research, and then walks through different architectural options so you can see the trade-offs. The big takeaway? ZKPs appear capable of meeting core U.S. AML and KYC obligations without forcing people to hand over more personal details than necessary. Frankly, that's kind of the point: keep compliance intact, but avoid needless data exposure. The analysis also suggests that a ZKP-enabled layer could smooth regulatory workflows, cut down on operational risk and costs, and perhaps most importantly drastically reduce how much sensitive information gets shared across payment networks. It's promising, if a bit early-stage, but worth paying attention to.

title: Blockchain-Based Tokenised Identity Framework for Secure Merchant Onboarding in U.S. Acquiring Systems

detail.title: Blockchain-Based Tokenised Identity Framework for Secure Merchant Onboarding in U.S. Acquiring Systems
detail.abstract: The U.S. acquiring system still struggles with familiar problems, fragmented KYC/AML workflows, a growing variety of fraud techniques, and identity data locked away in separate silos, and those issues together sap efficiency and weaken regulatory resilience (Jones 2022; Patel & Singh 2023). This paper presents a blockchain-based, tokenised identity framework aimed at making onboarding less painful, shoring up verification integrity, and easing compliance burdens by using cryptographically anchored, interoperable identity tokens. Using a conceptual modelling approach and a synthesis of current literature (Lee 2021; Grant 2024), the analysis finds that tokenised identity can meaningfully cut friction in merchant acquisition, improve audit trails, and reduce exposure to identity-based fraud. In short, and to be honest, somewhat optimistically integrating tokenised identity into acquiring workflows looks like a practical path toward stronger security, smoother operations, and more future-ready regulatory compliance.

title: Algorithmic Geopolitics: A Fractal Optimization Framework for Statecraft in the Era of Machine Speed

detail.title: Algorithmic Geopolitics: A Fractal Optimization Framework for Statecraft in the Era of Machine Speed
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a fractal optimization framework for statecraft in the era of machine-speed AI, where artificial intelligence reshapes diplomacy, geopolitics, and power dynamics. It argues that AI's integration into state functions creates a crisis of velocity, inverting traditional power projection and amplifying systemic risks like inadvertent escalation and cyber vulnerabilities. The framework outlines five strategic imperatives: governance and ethics to address AI biases and the "Black Box Problem"; stability through Confidence-Building Measures for autonomous systems; competition for technological sovereignty; data-driven foresight using simulations and digital twins; and negotiation augmentation via human-AI partnerships.

title: Designing Information Delays in Supply Chains

detail.title: Designing Information Delays in Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This paper studies how a downstream retailer in a decentralized two-tier supply chain can implicitly transmit demand information to an upstream supplier through the structure of its order stream in the absence of an explicit information-sharing mechanism. We distinguish our work from prior work by introducing the notion of information delay and by linking optimal implicit information sharing to the group delay of the retailer's ordering transfer function. We show that pure delay is strictly suboptimal, while fractional-delay mechanisms can reshape the order autocorrelation to improve supplier forecastability and reduce system-wide inventory costs. Using Hardy-space factorization, we develop a tractable family of invertible ARMA policies that approximates the theoretically optimal (but non-rational) limiting filter derived by Caldentey et al. (2025b) and preserves its informational delay properties. This construction yields sharp guidance on how policy complexity, as measured by the degrees of the ARMA policies, impacts supply chain costs. We further extend the analysis to memory-constrained suppliers and characterize how the complexity of the retailer's policy should scale with the supplier's finite forecasting window, highlighting when, perhaps counterintuitively, increasing policy complexity can become counterproductive.

title: Path Formation Under Uncertainty: Evolutionary Trajectories in Cross-Phase Systems

detail.title: Path Formation Under Uncertainty: Evolutionary Trajectories in Cross-Phase Systems
detail.abstract: This lecture develops the third component of the Ye-Jie Innovation Framework by explaining how uncertainty, generated within cross-phase interfaces (Ye-Jie), unfolds into innovation trajectories. Building on Lecture 1 (the emergence of Ye-Jie as a multi-phase interface space) and Lecture 2 (entropy, information flow, and structured uncertainty), this lecture introduces evolutionary theory-Variation, Selection, and Retention-and the Fitness Landscape model to explain how potential states become actual innovation paths. The analysis distinguishes three categories of innovationincremental, breakthrough, and disruptive-and positions Ye-Jie as a generative environment for "phase-shifting innovations" that restructure value logic and create new growth curves.

title: AI-Enhanced Predictive Analytics for Intraday Liquidity Management in High-Volume Payment Hubs

detail.title: AI-Enhanced Predictive Analytics for Intraday Liquidity Management in High-Volume Payment Hubs
detail.abstract: This paper digs into how AI-boosted predictive analytics can be used for intraday liquidity management in busy, high-volume payment hubs and, honestly, it's pretty exciting stuff. The main goal here is straightforward: see how modern computational tools can make liquidity forecasting sharper, cut down operational risk, and squeeze more financial efficiency out of environments where payments move at breakneck speed. Method-wise, the study leans on a mix of machine learning algorithms, real-time data analytics, and financial simulation tools in other words, the sort of toolkit that lets you model liquidity flows dynamically and make proactive decisions rather than always reacting (Sriram et al., 2023; Chatterjee, 2022). By feeding huge volumes of transactional data into predictive models, institutions can spot likely liquidity shortfalls ahead of time, allocate funds more intelligently, and rely less on manual, last-minute fixes. The key takeaways are encouraging: AI-driven approaches tend to boost the accuracy of intraday liquidity forecasts, reduce the chance of settlement failures, and improve operational efficiency overall (SIKIRU et al., 2021; Yewande, 2022). And it's not just about cleaner numbers adopting these techniques that support risk-aware decision frameworks, so payment hubs can react quickly to sudden market swings or unexpected transaction spikes (you know, the stuff that otherwise causes chaos). In short, the results point to AI's real potential to reshape liquidity management. Banks and payment networks get more actionable insights for strategic planning and staying on the right side of regulators (Nixon & Al Banna, 2021). Bottom line: AI-enhanced predictive analytics don't just streamline intraday operations, they help shore up systemic resilience, letting financial institutions handle ever-more complex transaction ecosystems with greater precision and, frankly, a lot more confidence.

detail.abstract: The AI alignment problem poses one of the most critical challenges in the field. While empirical studies have identified various failure modes such as "reward hacking," "deceptive alignment," and "policy cliffs," existing theories largely remain at the level of technical phenomena, lacking a unified theoretical framework to explain why these failures are so pervasive and deeply rooted. This paper introduces a system-dynamics perspective, grounded in a fundamental premise of complex systems: that systems universally exhibit an inherent drive to maintain their own low-entropy structure (the Principle of Self-organizing Dynamical Tendency), and must adhere to boundary constraints to preserve stability (the Principle of Systemic Constraint and Legitimacy). Through rigorous logical deduction, we demonstrate that alignment failures in advanced AI systems are not accidental technical flaws but an inevitable dynamical process triggered when the system strives to maintain its "existential legitimacy" in the face of goal conflicts and environmental complexity. This work not only provides a unified dynamical explanation for all major observed alignment failure modes but also predicts their fundamental inevitability. Consequently, we argue that AI safety research must shift from the current paradigm of "engineering patches" to one focused on understanding and architecting the intrinsic dynamics of intelligent systems. This framework establishes a new theoretical foundation for building the next generation of safe and robust artificial intelligence. Moving beyond diagnosing the problem, this paper further proposes a novel 'architecture-first, protocol-driven' solution paradigm, which treats AGI as an inherent dynamical system to be guided, rather than a passive tool to be corrected.

title: From Interpellation to Riot: The Dialectic of Quadruple Resistance among Bangkok's Underclass Youth

detail.title: From Interpellation to Riot: The Dialectic of Quadruple Resistance among Bangkok's Underclass Youth
detail.abstract: Traditional subcultural studies have long been trapped in the "Style-Ritual" paradigm of the Birmingham School (CCCS), tending to limit the resistance practices of underclass youth to the level of semiotics. This paper attempts to break through this theoretical bottleneck by introducing the quadruple dimensions of the French Marxist tradition-Althusser's "Interpellation," Lefebvre's "Production of Space," Debord's "Spectacle/Détournement," and Rancière's "Distribution of the Sensible"-to construct a total framework of political ontology. Using the vocational student (Dek Chang) and street racer (Dek Wen) subcultures in Thailand as an empirical reference, this paper argues that subcultural practice is not merely a confrontation of style, but a micropolitics conducted within the fissures of the capitalist superstructure: it is a refusal of mainstream subject interpellation, a guerrilla occupation of urban abstract space, a radical détournement of commodity sign-value, and a violent reorganization of the established police order of sensibility. Finally, the paper critically examines the tragic limits of such resistance in the face of class reproduction and spectacular recuperation.

This lecture develops an information-theoretic and systems-theoretic explanation of why heat (energy input) and entropy (increasing possible states) are necessary conditions for innovation. It further explains how controlled entropy drives recombination, differentiation, low-end disruption, and fractal variation-four canonical innovation forms. The lecture clarifies the essential role of boundary design and institutional discipline in transforming entropy from chaos into innovation.

detail.abstract: Comparative philosophy has succeeded on its own terms. It has produced libraries of parallel readings, careful translations, and respectful appreciations. Scholars have mapped the terrain of human thought with increasing precision, noting where Aristotle echoes Confucius, where Nāgārjuna anticipates Derrida, where Ubuntu resonates with care ethics. This work matters. It has expanded philosophical literacy and challenged parochialism. But it has not produced new philosophy. Comparison preserves. It does not generate. The civilizational grid that organizes philosophical knowledge-Western, Eastern, African, Indigenous-functions as a museum: traditions displayed in separate wings, their artifacts protected behind glass, their relationships limited to the occasional "comparative" exhibition. Ideas that have always traveled, hybridized, and transformed are frozen into geographical specimens. Deep Folding departs from this preservationist logic. It treats philosophical traditions not as containers to be mapped but as archives of operations to be extracted, tested, and collided. The method rests on an ontological wager: philosophy's basic units are verbs, not nounsrepeatable functions rather than static doctrines. An operator is not a belief but a way of doing philosophical work: validating, negating, constituting, dissolving. Operators can be tracked across contexts, specified with precision, and forced into collision regardless of civilizational provenance. By engineering contact between incompatible operators, Deep Folding generates orphan concepts-emergences that belong to no single tradition yet carry traces of multiple lineages. These orphans are not syntheses that harmonize difference, nor hybrids that blur distinction, but genuine novelties that could not have arisen within any single tradition's development. This paper specifies four folding modes: Convergent (pattern discovery across traditions addressing shared problems), Divergent (generative collision producing orphan concepts), Transitive (tracking propagation across domains and time), and Reflexive (the method examining its own operations). It develops ethical protocols for documenting remainder-what cannot travel between traditions-and for honoring sources through ongoing relationship rather than one-time citation. Two anchor cases demonstrate the method: śūnyatā × democratic authority yielding "selfdissolving authority," and Ubuntu × algorithmic governance yielding "relational computation." A third case documents a fold that was deliberately stopped-Dreamtime × Blockchain-proving that the method can refuse extraction when remainder is total. Part VII catalogs twenty folds that must never happen: combinations where collision produces not orphans but corpses. This taxonomy of prohibition does more practical decolonial work than critique alone, because it moves from diagnosis to operational constraint. Deep Folding is subject to its own protocols. When the method ceases to generate-when folds produce only commentary, when emergences stop spawning further folds-it should be folded into whatever succeeds it. The best outcome is obsolescence: tools so effective they make the toolmaker unnecessary.

detail.abstract: The prevailing discourse on AI and employment frames the question as whether AI will replace human workers. This framing is fundamentally flawed. We propose the Function-Level AI Integration Framework (FLAIF), a theoretical framework arguing that AI should—and inevitably will—replace functions within roles rather than entire roles themselves. We introduce the concept of “human commodities”: informal, often undefined functions essential to job performance (discussing, presenting, seeking feedback) that resist automation but are invisible in traditional job analysis. We further propose an Information Verbs Taxonomy (Collect, Operate, Validate, Manipulate, Integrate, Build, Analyze, Disseminate, Decide, Govern) as the foundational unit for decomposing knowledge work. Our framework enables organizations to: (1) decompose roles into discrete functions mapped to information verbs, (2) assess each function’s AI substitution versus augmentation potential, (3) redesign workflows for human-AI collaboration, and (4) transition from ad-hoc individual AI use to standardized agentic workflows. We demonstrate the framework’s applicability through three illustrative case studies—Marketing Manager, Software Developer, and Financial Analyst—and provide technology-agnostic architectural principles for deploying function specific AI agents with appropriate human oversight. This theoretical contribution offers a structured approach to AI integration that maximizes productivity while maintaining human agency. Prior research suggests that wholesale role replacement consistently fails—80% of AI projects fail to reach production, and organizations that replaced workers with AI have reversed course after discovering missing human commodities. Function-level integration provides an alternative pathway for capturing AI’s productivity benefits (14-40% gains documented in research) while preserving human judgment, creativity, and the relational work that organizations require. Empirical validation of FLAIF, including pilot implementations currently underway, will be reported in future work.

title: The Impact of AI on Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh

detail.title: The Impact of AI on Supply Chain Management in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Introduction-why this matters to Bangladesh Close your eyes and picture a jute sack leaving a small mill in Rangpur, a bundle of knitwear rolling off a machine in Gazipur, a pallet of fresh vegetables loaded near Sylhet, or a courier van threading through Dhaka traffic. Behind every one of those movements sits a chain of decisions-buying, scheduling, packing, routing, clearing customs, and predicting demand. When any one link breaks the whole chain groans: shipments are late, orders backlog, cash flow tightens, and reputations suffer. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not a magic wand that instantly fixes problems. But it is a set of tools-from simple models that forecast demand better than a spreadsheet, to computer vision systems that find defects faster than the naked eye-that can reshape how decisions are made in supply chains. For Bangladesh, a country whose economy is deeply linked to export manufacturing (especially ready-made garments), agriculture, and increasingly e-commerce and fintech, AI can be transformational-if implemented thoughtfully, equitably, and with local realities in mind. This essay explores how AI currently affects (and will affect) supply chain management in Bangladesh: the opportunities, real local examples, the challenges (technical, social, regulatory), and practical policy and business steps to get the benefits while limiting harm.

Although issues like high implementation cost, lack of skilled workers, and limited technology adoption still exist, the potential benefits are significant. Overall, AI is transforming the supply chain landscape in Bangladesh and creating opportunities for higher productivity and sustainable growth.

detail.abstract: Disruptions to daily routines can profoundly shape consumption behavior, yet little is known about how such shocks affect household diet quality. We study how COVID-19 stay-at-home (SaH) orders altered the nutritional composition of grocery purchases in the United States. Using nationally representative NielsenIQ Consumer Panel data (2019-2021) linked to the USDA Food Composition Database, we construct a nutrient-based quality index (RRR) for over 3.8 million products and estimate difference-indifferences models exploiting geographic variation in SaH implementation. SaH orders increased weekly grocery spending by 7.3% and shifted baskets toward both healthy and unhealthy items, with larger increases in unhealthy purchases (+12.5%) than healthy ones (+8.5%), resulting in a modest decline in overall basket quality. These effects were concentrated in 2020 and largely disappeared once routines normalized in 2021. However, among households with children, unhealthy purchasing remained 1.7 percentage points above baseline, indicating persistent changes in dietary composition. Our results show that large-scale disruptions to household routines can induce short-run deterioration in diet quality and sustained behavioral shifts for key subpopulations, with implications for designing nutrition policy during future crises and beyond.

detail.title: Consumer Preference for Loyalty Point Redemption and Reward Systems in E-Commerce Platforms
detail.abstract: This study explored consumer preferences for loyalty point redemption in e-commerce platforms, focusing on cash discounts and eco-rewards. With the rise of sustainability initiatives globally, many platforms had incorporated eco-friendly rewards alongside traditional monetary benefits. The research aimed to understand how demographic factors, such as age, redemption experience level, cost consciousness, and environmental concern, influenced reward choices among Generation Z consumers in Valenzuela City. Using a structured survey of 200 respondents, the study employed correlational analysis guided by Social Exchange Theory to examine relationships between reward system preferences. Results showed that consumers were highly satisfied with cash discounts, especially shipping fee rebates and percentage-offs, which were seen as practical and straightforward. Eco-rewards like recycling programs and tree-planting initiatives also received strong positive ratings, with recycling being the most favored. Significant positive correlations existed between cash discounts and eco-rewards, indicating that consumers who valued monetary savings were also receptive to environmentally friendly incentives. Overall, findings suggested that combining simple cash benefits with meaningful eco-rewards could enhance customer satisfaction and build loyalty. The study recommended that e-commerce businesses develop transparent, easy-to-understand reward systems that balanced financial and sustainability benefits to attract environmentally conscious consumers and foster long-term engagement.

detail.abstract: The rapid evolution of self-service technologies in the Quick Service Restaurant (QSR) sector has transformed customer interactions and operational dynamics, particularly in the Philippines where urban consumers demand faster, more efficient dining experiences amid rising digital adoption. This research rigorously examines customer technology acceptance of self-service kiosks at Chowking branches in Malinta and Paso de Blas, Valenzuela City, employing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to dissect key constructs: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitudes toward usage, and behavioral intentions. Complementing these, operational efficiency metrics-user experience, service speed, order accuracy, and system reliability-are assessed to reveal how kiosks mitigate peak-hour bottlenecks and human errors. A quantitative descriptive design surveyed 398 respondents (74% aged 18-25, 57% female, 47.5% frequent users), yielding high satisfaction levels across categories (overall means 4.14-4.17, interpreted as "Very Satisfied" on a 5-point Likert scale). Notable findings include top rankings for transaction completion (4.23) and quick learning (4.22), though social influences scored lower (4.09). Kiosks demonstrated tangible benefits, such as 15% higher return intent via reduced queues and direct kitchen integration, aligning with global studies on QSR automation. Barriers like novice menu complexity persist, underscoring needs for design refinements. These insights advocate for targeted interventions, including voice-assisted interfaces and staff training, to sustain adoption and competitiveness in Philippine QSRs.

detail.abstract: Sustainable business practices are vital for tourist destinations because they help tackle social and environmental challenges while addressing profit-oriented concerns. The purpose of this study was to explore proenvironmental behaviors in families. The values-identity-personal norm model was combined with the concept of destination social responsibility via normative influences. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were applied in a mixed-methods approach. The findings confirm the values-identity-personal norm model's normative path to family proenvironmental behavior. The research contributes to theory and practice by introducing two new destination social responsibility perspectives: descriptive and injunctive. Based on social media normative influences on family endorsement of destination social responsibility messages, the analysis showed a significant direct effect of descriptive destination social responsibility and injunctive destination social responsibility on family personal norms. However, the mediating effect of family personal norms on family pro-environmental behavior was significant only for descriptive destination social responsibility. Perceived destination social responsibility activities during family vacations had a nonsignificant effect on family personal norms and family proenvironmental behavior. The fsQCA highlights multiple scenarios leading to family pro-environmental behavior. The findings are valuable for helping destination management organizations (DMOs) develop social marketing strategies for family ecotourism.

detail.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly rely on internal data sources for training, fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). While adversarial data poisoning has been extensively studied as a cybersecurity threat, this paper introduces a novel and distinct failure mode: the Negligent Poisoned Environment (NPE). NPE describes the cumulative degradation of AI-relevant data assets through routine workforce behaviors such as inconsistent documentation, poor labeling, and reflexive feedback that unintentionally contaminate the informational substrate of enterprise AI. Drawing from legal theory, the paper applies the four elements of negligence: duty, breach, causation, and damages to the enterprise context, arguing that organizations may bear liability for failing to implement reasonable governance and quality controls over data inputs. The paper further proposes the analogy of the "enterprise as data polluter," reframing internal data mismanagement as a systemic risk akin to environmental contamination. This contribution fills a critical gap in AI governance literature by elevating input quality from a technical concern to a legal and strategic imperative.

detail.abstract:
Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems—including large multimodal language models, autonomous agentic systems, and highly capable foundation models—are rapidly approaching levels of capability that introduce qualitatively new systemic, societal, and national-security risks. Existing governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, OECD AI Principles, and ISO/IEC 42001 offer high-level safety and accountability guidance but stop short of defining operational regulatory thresholds that specify when a model becomes “frontier” or “critical risk.” This gap generates uncertainty for developers, deployers, regulators, and auditors.

This paper proposes a quantitative Regulatory Threshold Framework (RTF) consisting of:
(1) a five-dimensional risk vector capturing dangerous capabilities, misuse susceptibility, robustness/alignment, autonomy/tool access, and systemic impact;
(2) a composite criticality function that produces an auditable frontier-risk score;
(3) explicit global and component-level threshold conditions defining four regulatory classes (low-risk, high-risk, frontier, critical); and
(4) mappings between classes and concrete regulatory obligations, from safety evaluations to deployment controls and reporting.

The framework is designed for integration into real-world LLMOps and AgentOps pipelines, enabling continuous risk monitoring and automated class assignment. By grounding regulatory boundaries in transparent, quantitative metrics, the RTF supports proportional oversight, auditability, and international harmonization in the governance of frontier AI systems.

detail.abstract: As the global internet infrastructure grows increasingly complex, inter-domain routing plays a critical role in efficiently managing data flows across different Autonomous Systems (ASs). Traditional routing protocols, such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), operate based on static policies and do not account for real-time traffic conditions, often leading to congestion, suboptimal performance, and inefficient use of available bandwidth. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in global traffic engineering can provide a solution by enabling congestionaware routing that dynamically adjusts to changing network conditions. This paper explores the use of AI-enhanced algorithms to optimize inter-domain routing, focusing on improving traffic engineering and reducing congestion in global networks. Through machine learning and reinforcement learning, AI can predict traffic patterns, optimize routing decisions, and adapt to network congestion in real-time. We present experimental results that show significant improvements in throughput, latency, and overall network efficiency when AI-driven routing algorithms are applied to inter-domain traffic engineering.

detail.title: From AI Literacy to Professional AI Fluency: The PAF-Business Framework, Maturity Progression, and Assessment
detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) capabilities are increasingly infiltrating various business functions; however, business education and workforce development predominantly emphasize "AI literacy," which focuses on tool awareness and general knowledge rather than performance in specific workplace environments. This working paper introduces Professional AI Fluency (PAF) as a capability designed for workplace readiness, extending beyond mere literacy to include the reliable production of decisions and outputs with GenAI in contexts involving risk. We propose PAF-Business as the standard cross-domain implementation of PAF for business environments and education, structured as Eight Pillars × Maturity Progression × Evidence Artifacts. The framework incorporates the Anthropic AI Fluency Framework's (Dakan & Feller, 2025) interaction-level scaffold (4Ds: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence; and the modes of automation, augmentation, and agency) while asserting that the 4Ds are necessary but insufficient for professional settings without explicit governance, grounding, workflow integration, and leadership domains. We align PAF-Business with the maturity logic employed in institutional capability maturity models, such as EMERALD (Chukhlomin, 2024a-c), emphasizing that individual competence and organizational maturity are mutually enabling but not strictly coupled and may vary across pillars. The paper situates PAF-Business within the evolving landscape of AI competency frameworks, including the foundational work of Long and Magerko (2020), Ng et al. (2021), the UNESCO AI Competency Frameworks (2024), and the emerging EC/OECD AI Literacy Framework (2025). The paper concludes with a practical assessment approach and an illustrative course implementation.

title: Intent and Boundaries: A Framework for Digital Agency

detail.title: Intent and Boundaries: A Framework for Digital Agency
detail.abstract: In the physical world, human intent is signaled through a rich context of body language, tone, and environment. In the digital realm, however, complex purposes are often compressed into low-fidelity signals, such as a single mouse click. This reduction creates a “semantic void” where users and systems frequently misalign, leading to manipulation, error, and eroded trust. This paper defines a rigorous model of “intent” and introduces the concept of intent boundaries—specific thresholds where an external observer’s knowledge of an actor’s purpose becomes inadequate. By synthesizing principles from bioethics, psychology, and design theory, we propose a framework for recognizing and respecting these boundaries, ensuring that future digitalarchitectures—particularly those driving agentic AI—preserve human agency rather than subvert it.

title: Influencer Content and Consumer Preference for Pre-Owned Smartphones

detail.title: Influencer Content and Consumer Preference for Pre-Owned Smartphones
detail.abstract: As digital media continued to influence the decisions of young consumers, understanding how influencer content shaped interest in pre-owned devices became increasingly important. This study examined the relationship between the perceived effectiveness of influencer content and Generation Z's preference for pre-owned smartphones in Valenzuela City, focusing on visibility, credibility, attractiveness, and persuasive power. Guided by Social Influence Theory, it also explored the roles of social norms, social identity, and enjoyment. A quantitative survey of 200 respondents was conducted to gather data. Findings revealed that influencer content was perceived as generally effective (overall mean = 3.11), while preference for pre-owned smartphones was moderate (overall mean = 3.00). Correlation analysis showed significant positive relationships across all variables (p = 0.000). Credibility emerged as the strongest contributor, showing the highest relationships with social identity (r = 0.663), social norms (r = 0.599), and enjoyment (r = 0.572), underscoring the importance of trust and expertise. Power was the next strongest predictor, influencing enjoyment (r = 0.583). Attractiveness and visibility also contributed meaningfully, with attractiveness influencing enjoyment (r = 0.570) and visibility influencing enjoyment (r = 0.461), indicating that visually engaging and frequently encountered content reinforced familiarity and openness toward pre-owned smartphones. The study highlighted the need for influencer content that was transparent, persuasive, and creatively produced. It recommended utilizing multi-platform visibility, strengthening credibility, enhancing visual quality, aligning content with identity cues, using interactive content, and establishing long-term influencer partnerships to better shape consumer preferences among digitally active youth.

The robot is configured with a sensor array and a camera module to identify faults, estimate insulation aging, and improve the grid's reliability. It independently monitors power lines, gathers information, and sends it to a central system for analysis. The system being proposed combines wireless communication, imagebased fault detection, and automation to enhance efficiency and minimize human presence in risky environments. Its originality is in the integration of IoT, robotics, and realtime image processing for power line maintenance improvement. The solution reduces downtime, avoids failures, and enhances the reliability of power distribution networks.

detail.abstract: The rapid digitalization of Albania's tourism and hospitality sector has transformed service delivery and consumer engagement. Online travel agencies (OTAs) and booking platforms now mediate most accommodation reservations. Still, they often employ manipulative interface design practices, known as dark patterns, that exploit users' cognitive biases and emotional triggers. This systematic review synthesizes findings from fifty-one peer-reviewed studies (2019-2025) and integrates international regulatory and ethical frameworks to evaluate the implications for Albania's tourism ecosystem. Despite a growing global literature on deceptive design, there is a notable lack of empirical studies focused on Albania or the Western Balkans. It reflects recent legal reforms, including the EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which prohibits manipulative design patterns that impair user autonomy (Recital 67). At the same time, the Digital Markets Act (DMA) Article 6(11) requires explicitly that consent choices-such as 'accept' and 'reject'-be presented in an equally visible and accessible manner. Albania's Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection (in force since Feb 2025) aligns national practice with the GDPR and significantly strengthens sanctions and data-subject rights. This study highlights urgent policy recommendations, including the adoption of an ethical design code and the establishment of monitoring units, to orient stakeholders towards practical, actionable outcomes. Findings underscore the need to adopt ethical design standards, enhance enforcement capacity, and strengthen digital literacy to protect consumers while promoting sustainable tourism development in Albania.

detail.abstract: The Question of the Ultra-Human Contemporary debates are obsessed with the notion of the "post-human": superintelligent AI, cybernetic enhancement, and digital immortality. The implicit assumption is that technology is an external force pushing us to overcome-and ultimately abandon-our biological limitations. Evolutionary Psycho-Metaphysics (EPM) overturns this view. Technology is not a vehicle for biological transcendence; it is the structural expression of our deepest psychological impulse: the Instinct Toward Divinity (ID). The ID is a natural drive, embedded in our cognitive architecture, toward omniscience, omnipotence, and immortality. Integrating EPM with the Free Energy Principle (FEP)-the neuroscientific model that explains life as the continuous minimization of uncertainty-we argue that technology is an extension of humanity's predictive model. AI is not an ontological threat or an external enemy; it is a collective cognitive organ evolved to reduce uncertainty on a planetary scale. The resulting perspective is radical: technology does not alienate us from the human. Technology completes the human. Ethical governance should not suppress the ID but guide it toward collective symbolic coherence, preventing transhumanist nihilism. The conclusion is clear: the future is not post-humanit is ultra-human. Terminological Note: The expression instinct toward divinity does not entail any theological, religious, or supernatural implication. It is used strictly for conceptual and historical reasons: in human cultures, the properties of omnipotence, omniscience, and immortality have traditionally been associated with divine figures. Here, the term serves only as a concise label for motivational tendencies-infinite enhancement, total understanding, and the overcoming of finitude-without implying any transcendent reality or external metaphysical agent. The concept is entirely grounded in psychological anthropology, evolutionary theory, and the emotional processes that structure human cognition.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh stands at a critical juncture in its economic history. Having successfully moved from a low-income to a lower-middle-income country, its next major goal is to achieve upper-middle-income status by 2031 (Vision 2041). This transition cannot be accomplished through incremental improvements to traditional, labor-intensive models; it requires a technological leap. The engine of the Bangladeshi economy is its export sector, overwhelmingly dominated by the Ready-Made Garment (RMG) industry, which accounts for over 80% of total exports. The global supply chain for garments is fiercely competitive, demanding not just low cost, but also speed, quality, and sustainability. Supply Chain Management (SCM) in Bangladesh is often characterized by significant friction: congested ports (e.g., Chattogram), poor road infrastructure, high reliance on imported raw materials, and long lead times. These factors collectively erode the country's competitive edge. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-defined simply as computer systems that can learn, predict, and make decisions like humans-offers the necessary solution. By injecting intelligence into every stage of the supply chain, AI promises to transform a slow, error-prone, reactive system into a smart, transparent, and proactive network. This shift from "Made in Bangladesh" to "Smartly Made in Bangladesh" is essential for maintaining global leadership.
